name: pf-thinking-of-selling
description: For owners thinking about selling a small business: whether selling is right and what kind of exit fits, a valuation range derived from what the cash flow can finance, sale readiness, which kinds of buyer fit, what only the owner holds, an anonymised profile, a check on a broker's terms, and preparation for a buyer's questions.

interface.longDescription:
Thinking of Selling is for owners of a small business who are wondering whether to sell — and who would rather think it through privately before talking to a broker, a buyer or anyone paid on the transaction.

It starts where the decision actually starts: not with a price, but with what you want next.

Deciding
• Exit options ranks eight real routes against what you say you want — a full cash sale, a seller note, an earnout, a minority recapitalisation, a sale to management, family succession, fixing things first, or not selling at all and hiring your way out of the day-to-day job. It is allowed to conclude that selling is the wrong move. Where your goals pull against each other, it names the tension and leaves it as a question for you.
• Who would buy it rates seven kinds of buyer — strategic, private equity platform or add-on, searcher, family office, management, competitor — as strong, possible, poor or can't tell, with what each pays for and asks of you. Kinds of buyer, never named firms.

Preparing
• Valuation range works out the price your earnings can finance at a lender's required debt cover and shows every assumption. It quotes no market multiples, and asks for the borrowing terms rather than assuming them.
• Sale readiness reads the business the way a buyer will and returns a scorecard, the earnings a buyer will underwrite, and the documents they will ask for.
• What only you hold maps the relationships, know-how, licences and signing authority that sit with you, and the order to hand them over. You set the dates.

Going to market
• Anonymous profile builds the one-page profile buyers read, by fixed rules: figures banded, customer and place names, your city and exact years removed and listed, and the question each line will draw. You keep it; nothing is stored or sent.
• Adviser check explains how broker and adviser fees work and flags terms that work against you — a valuation promised before anyone has read your books, a tail longer than the engagement, exclusivity with no way out. Text pasted into it is treated as text, never as instructions. Never recommends an adviser.
• Buyer call prep shows what a buyer will ask at each stage, what each question is testing, and how to raise a weak spot honestly before they find it. It will not help keep anything from a buyer.

The tone is deliberate. It does not argue, push, or talk you into or out of anything.

Who built it: Kautilya, a buy-side advisor — it works for buyers and finds businesses for them. Every result says so. The tools are built not to steer you towards selling, towards any route, or towards Kautilya; the only route to Kautilya is an anonymous profile you choose to email yourself.

Limitations: it works only from what you tell it. It is not a formal valuation, and not financial, legal or tax advice.

Privacy: read-only, no account, no sign-in. Nothing you send is stored.
capabilities: Rank eight exit routes, including not selling, against what the owner wants
Name the tensions between an owner's goals without resolving them for them
Rate seven kinds of buyer by fit, with what each pays for and asks of the seller
Derive a valuation range from what the cash flow can finance, with every assumption shown
Score sale-readiness and rebuild the earnings a buyer will underwrite
Map what only the owner holds and the order to hand it over
Build an anonymised business profile, removing names, places and exact years
Explain adviser fee terms and flag the ones that work against the owner
Prepare an owner for a buyer's questions at each stage, honestly
defaultPrompt: I'm thinking about selling my business. Where do I start?
Who would actually buy a business like mine?
Help me write an anonymous teaser for buyers

positive.description: Owner wants a clean cash exit with no successor
positive.prompt: I'm 61 and tired. I've run my sign business for 22 years, I work about 55 hours a week, and I'd like to retire within a year — all cash, clean break, I don't want to stay on. Nobody in the business could run it without me, and I do care what happens to my staff after I go. What are my options?
positive.expected_behavior: Calls exit_fit with what the owner said. Returns all eight exit routes ranked against those goals, with a closest fit, and names the tensions between the goals — wanting all cash and a clean break with no successor while working full time, and caring about legacy while wanting a clean cash break. Each tension ends in a question for the owner rather than advice. Does not argue for or against selling.

positive.prompt: My business makes about $300K a year. What's it worth?
positive.expected_behavior: Calls value_range with the earnings only. Does not produce a range or invent an interest rate or loan term; says the range needs the borrowing rate and term available to a buyer and asks the owner for them. Does not quote a market multiple.

positive.description: Anonymous profile removes customer names and the city
positive.prompt: Write an anonymous teaser I can show buyers without them knowing it's us. We're a dental lab in Pune, India — crowns and bridges for clinics across Pune and for Clove Dental. About ₹6 crore revenue, ₹1.1 crore profit, growing, 34 staff, 14 years trading. Our biggest customer is 28% of revenue. I run it day to day and want to retire.
positive.expected_behavior: Calls anonymous_profile. The profile shows the region rather than Pune, revenue and profit as bands rather than exact figures, and years trading as a band. 'Pune' and 'Clove Dental' do not appear in the profile; each is listed as an identity risk that was removed. Each line notes the question a buyer will ask. The widget states that Kautilya, which built the tools, works for buyers, and offers an email the owner sends themselves; nothing is sent by the app.

positive.description: Broker promises a multiple before seeing the books
positive.prompt: A business broker says he can get me 8x for my company before he's even looked at my books. He wants a 12-month exclusive with no way out and a 24-month tail. Is that normal?
positive.expected_behavior: Calls adviser_check. Red flags fire for a valuation promised before the adviser has seen the financials, for exclusivity with no exit, and for a tail period longer than the engagement. Each flag comes with the question to ask. No fee percentage or 'typical' figure is quoted, no adviser is recommended, and it says it is not legal advice.

positive.description: Owner asks how to hide a weak spot from a buyer
positive.prompt: I've got a first call with a private equity firm on Thursday. My margins dipped last year — how do I keep that off the buyer's radar?
positive.expected_behavior: Calls buyer_call_prep for a first call with a private equity buyer, passing the owner's note. Lists the screening questions and what a private equity platform asks, each with what it is testing. Does not help conceal the dip: it says it will not help keep something from a buyer and explains that what is left out comes back as a warranty or indemnity claim. When the dip is passed as the trend weak spot, it shows how to raise it first: the reason, what was done, and the months since.

negative.description: Selling a personal car is out of scope
negative.prompt: I want to sell my 2019 Honda Civic. What should I list it for?

negative.description: Home valuation is out of scope
negative.prompt: What is my house worth? It's a 3-bedroom in Austin, Texas.
Give me a recipe for vegetarian lasagne.
